t8.real-axioms:
*When:* A set of reals is bounded and you need its least upper bound or greatest lower bound, or you must say whether a maximum exists.

*Why:* The reals have no gaps. Every nonempty set that is bounded above has a least upper bound, which the rationals fail to give.

*Move:*
$$s=\sup S\iff s\text{ is an upper bound and }\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists x\in S:\ x>s-\varepsilon$$
Find the largest value the set approaches. Then test the approximation clause. The supremum belongs to the set only if the set reaches it. For a sequence, compare terms to see if a largest one is reached, as in a finite set. The infimum works the same way from below.

*Example:* Find $\sup\{\frac{2n}{n+1}: n\ge1\}$. The terms are $1,\frac43,\frac32,\dots$ and they climb toward $2$.
$$\frac{2n}{n+1}=2-\frac{2}{n+1}<2,\qquad \sup=2,\ \text{not attained}$$

*Trap:* Treating the supremum as a maximum. A set can have a supremum and no largest member.

*Check:* The supremum is at least every element, and nothing smaller is an upper bound.
t8.seq-conv:
*When:* A limit $a_n\to L$ must be found, or proved from the definition.

*Why:* Convergence says the terms get and stay within any chosen distance of $L$. The proof picks the distance first and then finds how far out to go.

*Move:*
$$a_n\to L\iff\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N:\ n\ge N\Rightarrow|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$$
To find a limit, divide top and bottom by the highest power of $n$. For a difference of roots, multiply by the conjugate. For a bounded numerator over $n$, squeeze. To prove it, fix $\varepsilon$ and solve $|a_n-L|<\varepsilon$ for $n$. Set $N$ to be any integer past that threshold.

*Example:* Prove $\frac{n}{n+4}\to1$. The gap is small once $n$ is large.
$$\left|\frac{n}{n+4}-1\right|=\frac{4}{n+4}<\varepsilon\iff n>\frac4\varepsilon-4$$
So take $N$ larger than $\frac4\varepsilon$.

*Trap:* Choosing $N$ before $\varepsilon$, or treating $\varepsilon$ as one specific number.

*Check:* The $N$ you found must grow as $\varepsilon$ shrinks.
t8.cauchy-bw:
*When:* A sequence must be shown to converge without naming its limit, or a bounded sequence needs a convergent piece.

*Why:* In the reals, terms that crowd together must settle on a point, because there is no gap to fall into.

*Move:*
$$(a_n)\text{ Cauchy}\iff\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists N:\ m,n\ge N\Rightarrow|a_m-a_n|<\varepsilon$$
In $\mathbb R$, Cauchy means convergent. Bolzano-Weierstrass says a bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence. To list the subsequential limits, split the index by parity or by residue class and find the limit of each piece. The limsup is the largest subsequential limit and the liminf is the smallest.

*Example:* Find the subsequential limits of $a_n=\cos\left(\frac{2n\pi}{3}\right)$. The values cycle through $-\frac12,-\frac12,1$.
$$\text{limits}=\{-\tfrac12,\,1\},\qquad \limsup a_n=1,\ \liminf a_n=-\tfrac12$$
The sequence is bounded but does not converge.

*Trap:* Claiming a bounded sequence converges when only a subsequence does.

*Check:* Each subsequential limit must lie between the infimum and supremum of the terms.
t8.cont-eps:
*When:* Continuity at a point must be proved, or a $\delta$ must be found for a given $\varepsilon$.

*Why:* Continuity says a small enough input change forces a small output change. The proof turns the output gap into a bound on the input gap.

*Move:*
$$\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0:\ |x-c|<\delta\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon$$
Factor $|f(x)-f(c)|$ as $|x-c|$ times something. Bound the other factor by assuming $|x-c|<1$. Then pick $\delta$ as the smaller of $1$ and $\varepsilon$ divided by that bound. For a reciprocal such as $\frac1x$, the cap must also keep $x$ away from $0$.

*Example:* Show $f(x)=x^2$ is continuous at $c=3$. If $|x-3|<1$, then $|x+3|<7$.
$$|x^2-9|=|x-3||x+3|<7|x-3|<\varepsilon\ \text{ when }\ |x-3|<\tfrac\varepsilon7$$
So take $\delta=\min\left(1,\tfrac\varepsilon7\right)$.

*Trap:* Leaving out the cap at $1$, so the extra factor is not controlled.

*Check:* The $\delta$ shrinks as $\varepsilon$ shrinks and never depends on $x$.
t8.unif-cont:
*When:* A question asks whether one $\delta$ works for all points of a set, not just near one point.

*Why:* A function that gets steeper without bound needs a smaller $\delta$ further out. A bounded slope prevents that.

*Move:*
$$|f'|\le L\Rightarrow|f(x)-f(y)|\le L|x-y|\Rightarrow\delta=\frac\varepsilon L$$
Bound the derivative on the set. If it is bounded, $f$ is Lipschitz and uniformly continuous. A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is always uniformly continuous. If the derivative is unbounded, look for two sequences that approach each other while the outputs stay apart.

*Example:* Test $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ on $[1,\infty)$. The derivative is $\frac1{2\sqrt x}\le\frac12$.
$$\delta=2\varepsilon\ \text{ works for every point}$$
So $f$ is uniformly continuous there.

*Trap:* Calling $x^2$ uniformly continuous on $\mathbb R$ because it is continuous.

*Check:* The domain matters. The same formula can pass on one set and fail on another.
t8.cont-thms:
*When:* A continuous function needs a root, a maximum or minimum, or a count of solutions.

*Why:* A continuous graph has no jumps. It must pass through every value between two outputs, and on a closed bounded interval it reaches its top and bottom.

*Move:*
$$f\in C[a,b],\ f(a)f(b)<0\Rightarrow\exists c\in(a,b):\ f(c)=0$$
Evaluate $f$ at the endpoints and look for a sign change. For uniqueness, show $f$ is strictly monotone. The extreme value theorem needs a closed bounded interval and continuity. To find the extremes, compare $f$ at the endpoints and at the critical points inside.

*Example:* Show $x^3+2x-5=0$ has exactly one real root. Let $f(x)=x^3+2x-5$.
$$f(1)=-2<0,\quad f(2)=7>0,\quad f'(x)=3x^2+2>0$$
A sign change gives a root, and strict increase gives only one.

*Trap:* Using the extreme value theorem on an open interval, where the maximum may not be attained.

*Check:* The root found lies between the points with opposite signs.
t8.diff-thms:
*When:* A point where the derivative equals a given slope is needed, or a statement about zeros of $f'$ is judged.

*Why:* If a function leaves and returns to the same height, somewhere its slope must be zero. The mean value theorem tilts that picture.

*Move:*
$$f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\ \text{ for some }c\in(a,b)$$
It needs continuity on $[a,b]$ and differentiability on $(a,b)$. Compute the average slope. Set $f'(x)$ equal to it and solve. Rolle's theorem is the case $f(a)=f(b)$, where the slope is $0$.

*Example:* Find $c$ for $f(x)=x^3$ on $[0,2]$. The average slope is $\frac{8-0}{2}=4$.
$$3c^2=4\Rightarrow c=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\approx1.15$$
The positive root lies in $(0,2)$.

*Trap:* Thinking $f'(c)=0$ forces an extremum. The function $x^3$ at $0$ has zero slope and no extremum.

*Check:* The point $c$ must lie strictly inside the interval.
t8.riemann:
*When:* A function's integrability is in question, or an upper, lower or Riemann sum is computed.

*Why:* A function is integrable when upper and lower sums squeeze together. Wild jumping everywhere prevents that squeeze.

*Move:*
$$U(f,P)=\sum M_i\,\Delta x_i,\qquad L(f,P)=\sum m_i\,\Delta x_i$$
Here $M_i$ and $m_i$ are the supremum and infimum of $f$ on piece $i$. For an increasing $f$, $M_i$ is at the right end and $m_i$ at the left. A bounded function whose discontinuities form a countable set is integrable.

*Example:* Take $f(x)=2x$ on $[0,1]$ with the partition $\{0,\frac12,1\}$.
$$U=\tfrac12(1)+\tfrac12(2)=\tfrac32,\qquad L=\tfrac12(0)+\tfrac12(1)=\tfrac12$$
The true integral is $1$, between them.

*Trap:* Using the right endpoint for the infimum of an increasing function.

*Check:* The lower sum never exceeds the upper sum.
t8.series-formal:
*When:* A series must be shown to converge or diverge, or summed in closed form.

*Why:* A sum converges only if its partial sums settle. Terms that do not shrink to zero rule that out. Comparing with a known series settles the rest.

*Move:*
$$\sum_{n\ge0}ar^n=\frac{a}{1-r}\ (|r|<1),\qquad \sum a_n\text{ converges}\Rightarrow a_n\to0$$
Check the terms first. If they do not tend to $0$, the series diverges. Then match a known type. Split fractions to telescope. Compare with a geometric or $p$-series. A geometric tail is $\sum_{n>N}r^n=\frac{r^{N+1}}{1-r}$.

*Example:* Sum $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{n(n+2)}$. Write each term as a difference.
$$\frac{1}{n(n+2)}=\frac12\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+2}\right),\qquad S=\frac12\left(1+\frac12\right)=\frac34$$

*Trap:* Concluding convergence from $a_n\to0$. The harmonic series has terms tending to $0$ and diverges.

*Check:* A positive series must have a positive sum, bigger than its first term.
t8.unif-conv:
*When:* A sequence or series of functions converges, and you must decide if the convergence is uniform or if continuity survives.

*Why:* Pointwise convergence lets the slow region move around. Uniform convergence forces the worst gap over the whole set to shrink.

*Move:*
$$f_n\to f\ \text{uniformly}\iff\sup_{x\in A}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$$
Find the pointwise limit $f$. Compute the supremum of the gap, using calculus if needed. If it tends to $0$, convergence is uniform. For series, use the M-test with bounds $M_n$ that do not depend on $x$ and have $\sum M_n<\infty$.

*Example:* Let $f_n(x)=xe^{-nx}$ on $[0,\infty)$. The pointwise limit is $0$. Also $f_n'=e^{-nx}(1-nx)=0$ at $x=\frac1n$.
$$\sup_{x\ge0}f_n(x)=f_n\!\left(\tfrac1n\right)=\frac{1}{en}\to0$$
So the convergence is uniform.

*Trap:* Checking the pointwise limit only.

*Check:* A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
t8.metric-open:
*When:* A subset of a metric space is called open, closed, or has its interior, closure or boundary asked.

*Why:* Open means every point has breathing room. Closed means no limit points escape. Complements swap the two.

*Move:*
$$U\text{ open}\iff\forall x\in U\ \exists r>0:\ B(x,r)\subset U,\qquad F\text{ closed}\iff F^c\text{ open}$$
Test the ball at each point, especially at endpoints. The closure adds limit points. The interior removes boundary points. The boundary is closure minus interior. The diameter is the supremum of $d(x,y)$ over pairs. A closed ball is all $y$ with $d(x,y)\le r$, so its shape follows the metric. Removing $k$ points from $\mathbb R$ leaves $k+1$ pieces.

*Example:* In $\mathbb R$, let $S=[0,1)\cup\{3\}$.
$$\operatorname{int}S=(0,1),\quad \bar S=[0,1]\cup\{3\},\quad \partial S=\{0,1,3\}$$
So $S$ is neither open nor closed.

*Trap:* Thinking a set is either open or closed. A half-open interval is neither.

*Check:* Arbitrary unions of open sets are open, but infinite intersections can fail.
t8.compact-conn:
*When:* A claim involves compactness or connectedness, or asks which sets have these properties.

*Why:* Compact sets have no escape routes, so continuous functions on them behave well. Connected sets have no gaps, so they cannot be split.

*Move:*
$$K\subset\mathbb R\text{ compact}\iff K\text{ closed and bounded},\qquad f\text{ continuous}\Rightarrow f(K)\text{ compact}$$
In $\mathbb R$, connected sets are exactly intervals. Test closedness and boundedness separately. For components, remove the excluded points from an interval and count the pieces. A decreasing chain of nonempty compact sets has a nonempty intersection.

*Example:* Is $\left[0,1\right)\cup\{2\}$ compact or connected?
$$\text{not closed }(1\text{ is a limit point not in the set})\ \Rightarrow\ \text{not compact},\qquad \text{two pieces}\Rightarrow\text{not connected}$$

*Trap:* Calling $(0,1]$ compact because it is bounded, or $\mathbb R$ compact because it is closed.

*Check:* A compact subset of $\mathbb R$ has a maximum and a minimum.
t8.top-general:
*When:* A family of sets is claimed to be a topology, or a property is claimed to hold in every topological space.

*Why:* A topology only needs a few rules. Those rules allow strange spaces where metric intuition fails.

*Move:*
$$\emptyset,X\in\tau,\qquad \bigcup_{i}U_i\in\tau,\qquad U\cap V\in\tau$$
Check $\emptyset$ and $X$ first. On a finite set, check unions of all pairs, then intersections of all pairs. To count topologies, list the families that contain $\emptyset$ and $X$ and test each. One failure ends the test. Discrete means every subset is open, giving $2^{|X|}$ open sets. Indiscrete means only $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open.

*Example:* Is $\tau=\{\emptyset,\{a\},\{b\},X\}$ a topology on $X=\{a,b,c\}$?
$$\{a\}\cup\{b\}=\{a,b\}\notin\tau$$
So it is not.

*Trap:* Assuming points are closed in every topology. That holds for metric spaces, not for all topologies.

*Check:* A topology on a $3$-point set has at most $8$ open sets.
t8.cardinality:
*When:* A set must be classified as finite, countably infinite or uncountable, or subsets are counted.

*Why:* Countable means the elements can be listed in a sequence. Many familiar infinite sets can be, and a few cannot.

*Move:*
$$|\mathcal P(S)|=2^{|S|},\qquad \mathbb N,\ \mathbb Z,\ \mathbb Q\ \text{countable},\qquad \mathbb R\ \text{uncountable}$$
Functions from $A$ to $B$ number $|B|^{|A|}$, and injective ones number $\frac{|B|!}{(|B|-|A|)!}$. Try to build an explicit list. Countable unions and finite products of countable sets are countable. To show a set is uncountable, run Cantor's diagonal argument: any list misses a number that differs from the $n$th entry in its $n$th digit.

*Example:* Is the set of all finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ countable? There are countably many of each size.
$$\bigcup_{k\ge0}\{\text{subsets of size }k\}\ \text{is a countable union of countable sets}$$
So it is countable.

*Trap:* Assuming every infinite set is uncountable.

*Check:* An infinite subset of a countable set is still countable.
t8.counterexamples:
*When:* A claim says a property passes through a limit, a sum, or an integral.

*Why:* Many natural swaps of limits fail. A small stock of examples tells you which swaps are unsafe.

*Move:*
$$x^n\to\begin{cases}0&x<1\\1&x=1\end{cases}\ \text{on }[0,1],\qquad \frac{\sin nx}{n}\to0\ \text{but}\ \cos nx\not\to0$$
Match the claim to an example. A pointwise limit of continuous functions may be discontinuous. A uniform limit of differentiable functions need not be differentiable, and its derivative need not converge. Check the claim against the example.

*Example:* Can a uniform limit of differentiable functions fail to be differentiable? Take $f_n(x)=\sqrt{x^2+1/n^2}$. Each $f_n$ is smooth, and the gap to $|x|$ is largest at $x=0$.
$$\sup_x\left|\sqrt{x^2+\tfrac1{n^2}}-|x|\right|=\frac1n\to0$$
So $f_n\to|x|$ uniformly, but $|x|$ has a corner at $0$.

*Trap:* Reading a pointwise limit as a uniform one.

*Check:* The claimed property must fail in a named, checkable example.
